objectives.statement: Describe the effects a force can have and find the resultant of two or more forces acting along the same straight line.
Describe friction and drag as forces that oppose relative motion, and predict that an object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity in a straight line when the resultant force on it is zero.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise that a force is a push or a pull that has both a size and a direction.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Combining forces along a line only works once a force is treated as a signed quantity, not as a bare number.

prerequisites.statement: State that speed is distance travelled per unit time, and that a changing speed or a changing direction is called acceleration.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Deciding whether an object's motion is changing, without assuming it, is how you judge whether a resultant force is acting.

diagnostic_items.question: A toy car passes two marks 2.0 m apart in 4.0 s, then passes the next two marks (also 2.0 m apart) in another 4.0 s. Is its speed changing?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No, as far as these measurements show. The car covers equal distances (2.0 m) in equal times (4.0 s) on both stretches, so its average speed is the same, $0.50\,\mathrm{m/s}$, on each stretch.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner treats any motion at all as changing motion, instead of checking whether distance per unit time stays the same.
The learner does not use the two equal distance/time pairs already provided to compare the speeds.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether constant speed can be told apart from changing speed before that distinction is linked to resultant force.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Calculate the speed for each interval separately (distance divided by time) and compare the two values directly before deciding.

theory_blocks.title: Forces change motion; they are not needed to keep it going
theory_blocks.body:
A crate resting on the ground does not start moving by itself. It starts to move only when an unbalanced force acts on it.

More generally, a force can change an object's **size**, its **shape** or its **motion** (its speed or its direction of travel); this lesson concentrates on motion.

If a crate is pushed forward while friction drags backward on it, both forces act on the same crate at the same time, and what decides whether the crate speeds up, slows down,

or carries on unchanged is not either force alone: it is their combined effect, called the [[blue:**resultant force**]].

The resultant force is itself a force. It has a size and a direction, exactly like any of the individual forces that combine to produce it.

Once you know the resultant, you can ignore the individual forces and reason about the crate's motion using the resultant alone.

assets.caption: A crate pushed forward with 12 N while friction from the floor acts backward with 5 N. The two force arrows, drawn to a consistent scale, combine to a 7 N forward resultant.
assets.purpose: Make the combination of collinear forces into a single resultant visually explicit.

theory_blocks.title: Combining forces that act along the same line
theory_blocks.body:
When two or more forces act along the same straight line, their resultant is found like this:

1. Choose one direction as positive (for example, forward).
2. Add together every force that acts in the positive direction.
3. Add together every force that acts in the negative direction.
4. Subtract the negative-direction total from the positive-direction total. The sign of the answer tells you the direction of the resultant.

For example, a 12 N forward push and a 5 N backward friction force combine to a resultant of $12\,\mathrm{N}-5\,\mathrm{N}=7\,\mathrm{N}$ forward, as in the figure above.

This rule only combines forces that share the same line of action; forces at an angle to each other need a different method, which is outside this lesson.

When the positive-direction total exactly equals the negative-direction total, the resultant force is zero.

An object with zero resultant force stays at rest if it was already at rest, or continues at the same constant velocity in the same straight line if it was already moving: its motion does not change.

theory_blocks.title: Friction and drag: where they act and which way
theory_blocks.body:
**Friction** acts between two solid surfaces that are in contact and sliding (or trying to slide) against each other. **Drag** acts on an object moving through a liquid or a gas, including air resistance and water resistance. Both friction and drag oppose relative motion: they act against the direction the object is moving, or trying to move, relative to the surface or fluid, never with it.

Both also transfer some of the object's kinetic energy to the thermal (internal) energy store of the surfaces or the fluid, heating them, which is why a dragged object and the surface it slides over warm up slightly.

Because friction and drag oppose motion, they combine with a driving force along the same line using exactly the rule above: a 20 N forward pull with 7 N of friction and 5 N of drag,

both backward, gives a resultant of $20\,\mathrm{N}-7\,\mathrm{N}-5\,\mathrm{N}=8\,\mathrm{N}$ forward.

theory_blocks.title: Constant speed is not the same as no forces
theory_blocks.body:
It is tempting to think that an object moving at a steady speed in a straight line has nothing acting on it, because nothing about its motion seems to be changing.

In fact, [[blue:a driving force and a resistive force can both be present and both quite large, and still give a zero resultant if they are equal and opposite]].

The object's motion stays unchanged precisely because the forces are balanced, not because they are absent.

This rule applies to straight-line motion only: it tells you about speeding up, slowing down or staying the same along one line, and does not yet say anything about turning, which needs ideas beyond this lesson.

keywords.definition: The single force, with a size and a direction, that has the same effect as every individual force acting on an object combined.
Forces that act along the same straight line, so their combined effect can be found by addition and subtraction alone.
A force that opposes the relative motion between two solid surfaces in contact.
A force that opposes the motion of an object through a liquid or a gas.
The condition in which the forces acting on an object combine to a zero resultant force.

worked_examples.statement: **Pushing a trolley.** A trolley is pushed forward with a force of $10\,\mathrm{N}$. Friction between the wheels and the floor acts backward with $4\,\mathrm{N}$. Find the resultant force on the trolley and state its direction.
reasoning: Taking forward as the positive direction, the two forces are $+10\,\mathrm{N}$ and $-4\,\mathrm{N}$.
Combine them by subtracting the backward force from the forward force.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: adding the size of the backward force back onto the resultant, $6\,\mathrm{N}+4\,\mathrm{N}=10\,\mathrm{N}$, recovers the size of the forward push.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Adding the two forces to get $14\,\mathrm{N}$, instead of subtracting the backward force from the forward one.

worked_examples.statement: **Three forces on a sled.** A sled is pulled forward with $15\,\mathrm{N}$. Friction acts backward with $6\,\mathrm{N}$ and air resistance acts backward with a further $3\,\mathrm{N}$. Find the resultant force on the sled.
reasoning: Group the two backward forces together before combining with the forward pull, since both act in the same direction.
$6\,\mathrm{N}+3\,\mathrm{N}=9\,\mathrm{N}$ backward in total.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: adding the backward total back onto the resultant, $6\,\mathrm{N}+9\,\mathrm{N}=15\,\mathrm{N}$, recovers the size of the forward pull.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating the two backward forces as if they cancelled each other, instead of adding them together.

worked_examples.statement: **Cruising at a steady speed.** A car travels along a flat, straight road at a constant speed. The engine provides a driving force of $9\,\mathrm{N}$ forward (simplified for this example), and air resistance plus friction together provide $9\,\mathrm{N}$ backward. State the resultant force and explain why the car neither speeds up nor slows down.
reasoning: Find the resultant by combining the forward driving force with the backward resistive force.
$9\,\mathrm{N}$ forward and $9\,\mathrm{N}$ backward are equal and opposite, so they cancel exactly.
worked_examples.solution: The resultant force is $9\,\mathrm{N}-9\,\mathrm{N}=0\,\mathrm{N}$. With zero resultant force, the car's speed does not change: it continues at the same steady speed in the same straight line.
worked_examples.interpretation: This does not mean no forces act on the car. The driving force and the resistive force are both still present and equal in size; they simply combine to zero.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding that because the car keeps moving, there must be a leftover forward resultant force keeping it going.

worked_examples.statement: **A loaded trailer.** A trailer is pulled forward by a tractor with a force of $20\,\mathrm{N}$. As it moves, friction from the ground acts backward with $7\,\mathrm{N}$ and air resistance acts backward with $5\,\mathrm{N}$. (a) Find the resultant force on the trailer, stating its direction. (b) State, without calculating an acceleration, whether the trailer's speed is increasing, decreasing or staying constant.
reasoning: Combine the two backward forces first: $7\,\mathrm{N}+5\,\mathrm{N}=12\,\mathrm{N}$ backward.
Then combine this backward total with the forward pull.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $20\,\mathrm{N}-12\,\mathrm{N}=8\,\mathrm{N}$ forward. (b) Because the resultant force is not zero and acts forward, the trailer's speed is increasing.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: adding the backward total back onto the resultant, $8\,\mathrm{N}+12\,\mathrm{N}=20\,\mathrm{N}$, recovers the size of the forward pull.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming that because a pulling force is present at all, the trailer must already be moving at constant speed.

guided_exercises.statement: A shopping trolley is pushed forward with $18\,\mathrm{N}$. Rolling resistance acts backward with $11\,\mathrm{N}$. Find the resultant force on the trolley and state its direction.
hints: Decide which direction is positive and give each force a sign.
Combine the two forces, which act along the same line.
Check your answer by adding the backward force back onto it.
common_errors: Reporting 29 N by adding the two forces instead of finding their difference.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Decide which direction is positive and give each force a sign.

**Step 2 — Method:** Combine the two forces, which act along the same line.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $18\,\mathrm{N}-11\,\mathrm{N}=7\,\mathrm{N}$ forward. Check: $11+7=18$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer by adding the backward force back onto it.

guided_exercises.statement: Three forces act on a crate along the same line: $6\,\mathrm{N}$ forward, $6\,\mathrm{N}$ backward and $4\,\mathrm{N}$ forward. Find the resultant force on the crate.
hints: Add all the forward forces together first.
Add all the backward forces together.
Subtract the backward total from the forward total.
guided_exercises.answer: Forward total $=6+4=10\,\mathrm{N}$; backward total $=6\,\mathrm{N}$; resultant $=10-6=4\,\mathrm{N}$ forward.
common_errors: Cancelling the first 6 N forward against the 6 N backward and forgetting the remaining 4 N forward force.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Add all the forward forces together first.

**Step 2 — Method:** Add all the backward forces together.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Forward total $=6+4=10\,\mathrm{N}$; backward total $=6\,\mathrm{N}$; resultant $=10-6=4\,\mathrm{N}$ forward.

**Step 4 — Check:** Subtract the backward total from the forward total.

exercises.statement: A shopping trolley is pushed forward with a $22\,\mathrm{N}$ force. Friction acts backward with $9\,\mathrm{N}$. Find the resultant force and state its direction.

A boat's engine drives it forward with $30\,\mathrm{N}$. Water resistance acts backward with $12\,\mathrm{N}$ and a headwind acts backward with a further $8\,\mathrm{N}$. Find the resultant force on the boat.

A delivery van travels along a straight, flat road at a constant $15\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The driving force from its engine is $1200\,\mathrm{N}$ forward. State the size of the total backward resistive force acting on the van, and explain your reasoning.
exercises.full_solution: Constant speed in a straight line means the resultant force is zero, so the backward resistive forces must exactly balance the $1200\,\mathrm{N}$ forward driving force.

exercises.statement: An ice skater glides across very smooth ice, where friction is so small it can be treated as zero. No one is pushing the skater. Explain, in terms of resultant force, why the skater continues to glide at a steady speed in a straight line rather than slowing down.
exercises.answer: With friction taken as zero and no other horizontal force acting, the resultant horizontal force is zero, so the skater's speed and direction do not change: she keeps gliding at a steady speed in a straight line.
exercises.full_solution: This is the same zero-resultant idea as the cruising car, but here it is the near-absence of friction, rather than a balance of two large forces, that gives the zero resultant.

exam_questions.statement: A go-kart is driven forward by its engine with a force of $14\,\mathrm{N}$. Friction from the track acts backward with $5\,\mathrm{N}$ and air resistance acts backward with a further $3\,\mathrm{N}$. (a) Calculate the resultant force on the go-kart, stating its direction. (b) State what would happen to the go-kart's speed if the two backward forces increased until their total equalled $14\,\mathrm{N}$.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Backward total $=5+3=8\,\mathrm{N}$; resultant $=14-8=6\,\mathrm{N}$ forward. (b) The go-kart would travel at a constant speed, because the forward driving force and the total backward force would then be equal, giving a zero resultant.
mark_scheme: Adds the two backward forces: $5+3=8\,\mathrm{N}$.
Subtracts the backward total from the forward force: $14-8=6\,\mathrm{N}$.
States the direction of the resultant as forward.
States that the go-kart would travel at constant speed because the resultant would become zero.
common_errors: Giving only a magnitude in part (a) without stating the direction, which loses a mark.

exam_questions.statement: A delivery drone flies horizontally. Its rotors provide a forward thrust of $1500\,\mathrm{N}$. Air resistance acts backward. The drone travels at a constant horizontal speed. (a) State the size of the air resistance force. (b) The rotors' thrust increases to $1700\,\mathrm{N}$ while the air resistance stays the same. Calculate the new resultant force and describe what happens to the drone's horizontal speed.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $1500\,\mathrm{N}$, because the resultant force is zero at constant speed. (b) New resultant $=1700-1500=200\,\mathrm{N}$ forward; the drone's horizontal speed will increase, because the resultant force is no longer zero.
mark_scheme: States that constant speed means zero resultant, so air resistance $=1500\,\mathrm{N}$.
Calculates the new resultant: $1700-1500=200\,\mathrm{N}$.
States the direction as forward, in the direction of the thrust.
States that the drone's horizontal speed will increase because the resultant is no longer zero.
common_errors: Assuming the air resistance also increases to 1700 N, which would wrongly keep the resultant at zero without any evidence for it.

challenge_questions.answer: A complete answer links the physics concepts from resultant forces and motion to practical scenarios, using correct equations, SI units, and scientific reasoning.

mcq.stem: A box is pulled forward with $16\,\mathrm{N}$. Friction acts backward with $6\,\mathrm{N}$. What is the resultant force on the box?

options.text: $22\,\mathrm{N}$ forward
options.why_wrong: adds the two forces instead of subtracting the backward force from the forward one.

options.text: $10\,\mathrm{N}$ forward
$10\,\mathrm{N}$ backward
options.why_wrong: has the correct size but the wrong direction; the larger force is forward, so the resultant must be forward.

options.text: $6\,\mathrm{N}$ forward
options.why_wrong: reports the friction force rather than the resultant of the two forces.

mcq.explanation: $16-6=10\,\mathrm{N}$ forward, in the direction of the larger force.

mcq.stem: A sledge moves at a constant speed in a straight line across level snow. Which statement about the forces on it is correct?

options.text: No forces act on the sledge at all.
options.why_wrong: confuses a zero resultant with a complete absence of forces; friction and the pulling force are both still acting.

options.text: There must be a forward resultant force to keep the sledge moving.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes that constant motion itself needs an ongoing forward resultant force.

options.text: The forces on the sledge are balanced, so the resultant force is zero.
All the forces on the sledge must be equal to each other.
options.why_wrong: is not required: the forces only need to combine to a zero resultant, not be individually equal in size.

mcq.explanation: Constant speed in a straight line means the resultant force is zero: the forces are balanced, not absent.

mcq.stem: A swimmer pushes forward through water. In which direction does the water's drag force act on the swimmer?

options.text: In the same direction as the swimmer's motion.
options.why_wrong: describes drag acting with the motion, which would speed the swimmer up for no reason.

options.text: Vertically downward, regardless of the swimmer's direction.
options.why_wrong: confuses drag with weight; drag depends on the direction of motion through the fluid.

options.text: In a random, unpredictable direction.
options.why_wrong: ignores that drag is set by the direction of relative motion, not chosen at random.

options.text: Opposing the swimmer's motion through the water.

mcq.explanation: Drag, like friction, opposes the relative motion between an object and the fluid or surface it moves through or over.

mcq.stem: Three collinear forces act on a crate: $8\,\mathrm{N}$ forward, $3\,\mathrm{N}$ backward and $2\,\mathrm{N}$ backward. What is the resultant force?

options.text: $3\,\mathrm{N}$ forward
$13\,\mathrm{N}$ forward
options.why_wrong: adds all three forces together instead of treating the backward ones as negative.

options.text: $3\,\mathrm{N}$ backward
options.why_wrong: has the correct size but the wrong direction; the forward force is larger than the combined backward forces.

options.text: $5\,\mathrm{N}$ forward
options.why_wrong: combines only one of the two backward forces with the forward force and leaves the other out.

mcq.explanation: Backward total $=3+2=5\,\mathrm{N}$; resultant $=8-5=3\,\mathrm{N}$ forward.

mcq.stem: A squash ball is squeezed between two hands and is flattened, but it does not move anywhere. Which statement about the forces on the ball is correct?

options.text: No force acts on the ball, because the ball does not move.
options.why_wrong: assumes a force can only show itself as a change of motion; a force can also change an object's shape or size.

options.text: The forces change the shape of the ball.
The forces change the mass of the ball.
options.why_wrong: squeezing does not add or remove material, so the mass of the ball is unchanged.

options.text: The forces change the ball's direction of travel.
options.why_wrong: the ball stays where it is, so its motion does not change; what changes is its shape.

mcq.explanation: Forces may produce changes in the size, the shape and the motion of an object. Here the ball stays still, so the effect of the squeezing forces is a change of shape.

flashcards.front: What is a resultant force?
flashcards.back: The single force, with its own size and direction, that has the same effect as every individual force acting on an object combined.

flashcards.front: How do you combine two forces that act on the same straight line?
flashcards.back: Add together the forces that act in one direction, add together the forces that act in the opposite direction, then subtract one total from the other; the sign of the result gives the direction.

flashcards.front: If an object moves at a constant speed in a straight line, must a forward resultant force be acting on it?
flashcards.back: No. A zero resultant force gives rest or constant-velocity straight-line motion; the forces are balanced, not forward and not absent.

flashcards.front: How are friction and drag similar, and how do they differ?
flashcards.back: Both oppose relative motion and transfer energy by heating; friction acts between two solid surfaces in contact, while drag acts on an object moving through a liquid or a gas.

flashcards.front: A trolley moves at constant velocity, then someone adds a backward push. What happens to the resultant force and to the trolley's motion?
flashcards.back: The resultant force becomes nonzero and acts backward, so the trolley's speed decreases.

flashcards.front: State three effects a force can have on an object.
flashcards.back: A force may change an object's **size**, its **shape**, or its **motion** (its speed or its direction of travel).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A moving object needs a forward resultant force to keep moving.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Everyday pushing and pulling stops the moment the force stops, so it feels as if ongoing motion always needs an ongoing forward force.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner invents an extra forward force whenever an object is described as moving at constant speed.
misconceptions.correct_model: A zero resultant force is enough to keep an object moving at constant velocity in a straight line; no extra forward force is needed to sustain it.
misconceptions.remediation: Work through a case with two named forces that are equal and opposite, and show the constant speed follows from the zero resultant, not from either force alone.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Balanced forces mean that no force is acting at all.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A steady speedometer reading looks like nothing is happening, so it is tempting to conclude that nothing is acting.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a constant-velocity object as having 'no forces' rather than 'balanced forces'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Balanced forces means the individual forces are still present and still acting; they simply combine to a zero resultant.
misconceptions.remediation: Name each individual force out loud for a constant-velocity example, then show that they are equal and opposite before concluding the resultant is zero.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Friction always acts in the same direction as the object's motion.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Friction is only noticed when it visibly slows something down, so its direction is easy to confuse with the direction of travel.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner draws a friction or drag arrow pointing the same way as the velocity arrow.
misconceptions.correct_model: Friction and drag oppose relative motion: they act against the direction an object is moving (or trying to move) relative to the surface or fluid.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask which way the object is moving relative to the surface, then draw friction pointing the opposite way, every time, before calculating anything.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding two forces that act in opposite directions instead of subtracting one from the other.
common_mistakes.why: This treats every force as if it pointed the same way.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Assign a positive direction first, give every opposing force a negative sign, then add the signed values.

common_mistakes.mistake: Concluding that constant speed means no forces are acting.
common_mistakes.why: A steady speed feels like 'nothing is happening', so it is tempting to assume nothing is acting.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Name each force acting and show that they are equal and opposite before concluding the resultant is zero.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming friction or drag acts in the direction the object happens to be moving.
common_mistakes.why: Friction and drag are usually first noticed when they slow something down, so their direction is easy to mix up with the direction of travel.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Friction and drag oppose relative motion; draw them pointing against the direction of travel, never with it.

exam_notes: State both the size and the direction of a resultant force: a numerical answer without a stated direction rarely earns full marks.
When several forces act along the same line, group all the forces in each direction before subtracting one total from the other.
A zero resultant force is consistent with an object at rest or moving at constant velocity in a straight line: say which one applies to the situation in the question.

summary.big_idea: Whether an object speeds up, slows down or keeps a constant velocity in a straight line depends on the resultant of all the forces acting on it, not on any single force.
key_points: Forces along the same line combine by addition in one direction and subtraction in the opposite direction.
The resultant force is itself a force: it has both a size and a direction.
Friction and drag oppose relative motion and transfer energy by heating the surfaces or the fluid.
A zero resultant force means the forces are balanced, not absent, and the object stays at rest or keeps a constant velocity in a straight line.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Compare the resultant force, found by combining every force along the line of motion, with zero: zero means no change in motion; nonzero means the motion changes in the resultant's direction.

objectives.statement: Recall and use the relationship resultant force = mass × acceleration (F = ma), with mass in kilograms, acceleration in metres per second squared and force in newtons.
State that the acceleration produced by a resultant force acts in the same direction as that resultant force, which is not necessarily the direction the object is already moving.

prerequisites.statement: Find the resultant of two or more forces acting along the same straight line.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: F = ma uses the resultant force, not any single force acting on the object.

prerequisites.statement: State that acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes, measured in metres per second squared.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: F = ma predicts an acceleration, so its meaning as a rate of change of velocity must already be secure.

prerequisites.statement: Distinguish mass (how much matter an object contains, measured in kilograms) from weight (the force of gravity on it, measured in newtons).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: F = ma uses mass in kilograms; confusing mass with weight introduces a wrong unit directly into the equation.

diagnostic_items.question: A box is pulled forward along a bench with a force of $30\,\mathrm{N}$ while friction acts backward with $10\,\mathrm{N}$. What is the resultant force on the box?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $30\,\mathrm{N}-10\,\mathrm{N}=20\,\mathrm{N}$ forward, in the direction of the larger force.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner adds the two forces instead of subtracting the backward one, so opposing directions are not being given opposite signs.
The learner reports the friction force on its own rather than combining it with the pull.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: F = ma uses the resultant force, so a learner who cannot combine forces along a line will substitute one individual force into the equation instead.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Take forward as positive, write the two forces as $+30\,\mathrm{N}$ and $-10\,\mathrm{N}$, add the signed values, then state the direction of the answer.

diagnostic_items.question: A cyclist's velocity increases steadily from $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in $3.0\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the acceleration and say in words what that number means.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $a=(8.0-2.0)/3.0=2.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$: the velocity increases by $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ during every second.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner gives the change in velocity and does not divide by the time taken, treating acceleration as a change rather than as a rate of change.
The number is right but the unit is a velocity; acceleration is measured in metres per second squared.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: F = ma predicts an acceleration, so what acceleration means, and its unit, must be secure before the equation is used.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken, substitute the two velocities and the time separately, and check that the unit comes out as m/s².

diagnostic_items.question: A bag of sand has a mass of $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$. State its mass and calculate its weight on Earth, where $g=10\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The mass is $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$. The weight is the gravitational force on the bag: $W=mg=2.0\,\mathrm{kg}\times10\,\mathrm{N/kg}=20\,\mathrm{N}$.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner uses 'weight' for the reading from a balance; weight is a force and is measured in newtons.
The learner swaps the two quantities, giving the mass the value and the unit of the force.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: F = ma needs the mass in kilograms; substituting a weight in newtons for $m$ puts a wrong unit straight into the equation.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Say which quantity is measured in kilograms and which in newtons before substituting anything, and use $W=mg$ only when a force is asked for.

theory_blocks.title: The same force, different masses
theory_blocks.body:
Push an empty shopping trolley and a fully loaded one with exactly the same force, and they respond very differently: the empty trolley speeds up quickly, the loaded one barely picks up speed at all.

The force is identical in both cases, so the difference in how quickly each trolley's velocity changes must come from the trolley itself: specifically, from its mass.

This is the idea behind $F=ma$: for a given resultant force, [[blue:a larger mass produces a smaller acceleration]], and [[orange:a smaller mass produces a larger acceleration]].

The resultant force and the acceleration it produces point in the same direction, whatever direction the object happens to already be moving in.

assets.caption: A 50 N forward force and a 20 N backward force on a trolley combine to a 30 N forward resultant; the acceleration (dashed) acts in the same direction as that resultant, not simply forward because the trolley happens to be moving forward.
assets.purpose: Show, before and after combining the forces, that the acceleration takes the direction of the resultant rather than either individual force.

theory_blocks.title: F = ma
theory_blocks.body:
The resultant force on an object, its mass and the acceleration it produces are linked by

$$F=ma$$

where $F$ is the resultant force in newtons (N), $m$ is the mass in kilograms (kg) and $a$ is the acceleration in metres per second squared ($\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$).

These units are consistent with each other: substituting kilograms and metres per second squared into $F=ma$ gives newtons directly, with no conversion factor needed.

The equation can be rearranged to find any one quantity from the other two: $a=F/m$ or $m=F/a$. It applies to the resultant force only, for a fixed mass;

if the mass of the object itself is changing (such as a rocket burning fuel), this simple form no longer applies, which is outside this lesson.

theory_blocks.title: Find the resultant first, every time
theory_blocks.body:
When more than one force acts on an object, $F$ in $F=ma$ is never a single named force: it is the resultant of every force acting on the object, found exactly as in the previous lesson. A reliable method is always:

1. List every force acting on the object, with its size and direction.
2. Combine them into a single resultant force (the earlier addition/subtraction rule for collinear forces).
3. Only now substitute that resultant into $F=ma$.

Skipping step 2 and substituting one named force directly is the single most common error with this equation.

theory_blocks.title: The direction of acceleration
theory_blocks.body:
The acceleration calculated from $F=ma$ points in [[blue:the same direction as the resultant force]] used to calculate it, not in the direction the object happens to already be travelling.

If a forward-moving object experiences a backward resultant force, its acceleration is backward: the object slows down while still moving forward, and would eventually reverse direction if the backward resultant continued to act after it stopped.

keywords.definition: The relationship F = ma, linking the resultant force on an object, its mass and the acceleration produced.
The rate at which an object's velocity changes, measured in metres per second squared.
A measure of the amount of matter in an object, in kilograms, which does not depend on location.
The SI unit of force; one newton gives a mass of one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared.

worked_examples.statement: **A simple push.** A resultant force of $6.0\,\mathrm{N}$ acts on an object of mass $3.0\,\mathrm{kg}$. Calculate its acceleration.
reasoning: Rearrange $F=ma$ to make acceleration the subject: $a=F/m$.
Substitute the known values directly, since both are already in consistent SI units.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $3.0\,\mathrm{kg}\times2.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}=6.0\,\mathrm{N}$, which recovers the original force.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting to rearrange the equation and dividing mass by force instead of force by mass.

worked_examples.statement: **Finding the force.** A mass of $5.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ accelerates at $2.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Calculate the resultant force producing this acceleration.
reasoning: Here $F$ is already the subject of the equation, so no rearrangement is needed.
Substitute both values directly, keeping the units consistent.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $10\,\mathrm{N}/5.0\,\mathrm{kg}=2.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, which recovers the original acceleration.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing the answer in kilograms or leaving the unit out altogether.

worked_examples.statement: **Two forces, one object.** A $50\,\mathrm{N}$ forward force and a $20\,\mathrm{N}$ backward force act together on a $10\,\mathrm{kg}$ crate. Calculate its acceleration, and explain why neither $50\,\mathrm{N}$ nor $20\,\mathrm{N}$ alone can be substituted into $F=ma$.
reasoning: Find the resultant force first: $50\,\mathrm{N}-20\,\mathrm{N}=30\,\mathrm{N}$ forward.
Only now substitute this resultant into $F=ma$, rearranged for acceleration.
worked_examples.interpretation: Using $50\,\mathrm{N}$ alone would ignore the backward force entirely, and using $20\,\mathrm{N}$ alone would ignore the forward force; only the resultant, $30\,\mathrm{N}$, correctly represents the combined effect of both.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Substituting the larger named force (50 N) directly into F = ma without first subtracting the opposing force.

worked_examples.statement: **Braking.** A van of mass $1200\,\mathrm{kg}$, moving forward, brakes so that the resultant force on it is $1800\,\mathrm{N}$ backward. (a) Calculate its acceleration, stating its direction. (b) Suppose a forward force of $2000\,\mathrm{N}$ also acts on the van (for example, from a tow rope). Calculate the backward braking force now needed to give the same $1800\,\mathrm{N}$ backward resultant.
knowns: a forward force of $2000\,\mathrm{N}$ also acts in part (b)
reasoning: For (a), rearrange $F=ma$ for acceleration and substitute the resultant force and mass directly.
For (b), the resultant must still be $1800\,\mathrm{N}$ backward, so the backward braking force must exceed the $2000\,\mathrm{N}$ forward force by $1800\,\mathrm{N}$.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $a=1800\,\mathrm{N}/1200\,\mathrm{kg}=1.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ backward, so the van decelerates. (b) backward force $=2000\,\mathrm{N}+1800\,\mathrm{N}=3800\,\mathrm{N}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check for (b): resultant $=3800\,\mathrm{N}-2000\,\mathrm{N}=1800\,\mathrm{N}$ backward, as required.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Giving the acceleration in part (a) as forward, because the van is still moving forward while it brakes.

guided_exercises.statement: A resultant force of $10\,\mathrm{N}$ acts on a mass of $4.0\,\mathrm{kg}$. Calculate the acceleration produced.
hints: Write down F = ma and decide which letter you need to find.
Rearrange the equation before substituting any numbers.
Check your answer by multiplying it by the mass to see if you recover the original force.
common_errors: Writing a = m/F instead of a = F/m.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Write down F = ma and decide which letter you need to find.

**Step 2 — Method:** Rearrange the equation before substituting any numbers.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $a=10\,\mathrm{N}/4.0\,\mathrm{kg}=2.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Check: $4.0\times2.5=10$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer by multiplying it by the mass to see if you recover the original force.

guided_exercises.statement: A $0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$ trolley experiences a resultant force of $2.0\,\mathrm{N}$. Calculate its acceleration.
hints: Identify which quantity is the mass and which is the force before substituting.
Divide the force by the mass.
Check that your answer has the correct unit, m/s².
common_errors: Treating 0.50 kg as if it were 0.50 N and swapping the roles of mass and force.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Identify which quantity is the mass and which is the force before substituting.

**Step 2 — Method:** Divide the force by the mass.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $a=2.0\,\mathrm{N}/0.50\,\mathrm{kg}=4.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check that your answer has the correct unit, m/s².

exercises.statement: A mass of $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ accelerates at $3.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Calculate the resultant force producing this acceleration.
A car of mass $1500\,\mathrm{kg}$ experiences a resultant force of $4500\,\mathrm{N}$ forward. Calculate its acceleration.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $1500\times3.0=4500\,\mathrm{N}$.

exercises.statement: A cyclist and bicycle of total mass $60\,\mathrm{kg}$ pedal forward with $400\,\mathrm{N}$ while air resistance and friction together provide $250\,\mathrm{N}$ backward. Calculate the acceleration, stating its direction.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $60\times2.5=150\,\mathrm{N}$.

exercises.statement: A rocket-propelled test sled of mass $250\,\mathrm{kg}$ has a forward thrust of $3000\,\mathrm{N}$ and a backward drag of $500\,\mathrm{N}$. A different experiment uses the same sled design but doubles its mass by adding instruments, while the thrust and drag stay the same. First predict, without calculating, whether the new acceleration will be larger, smaller or the same, then calculate both accelerations to check your prediction.
exercises.answer: Doubling the mass for the same resultant force should halve the acceleration, since $a=F/m$.
exercises.full_solution: Resultant $=3000-500=2500\,\mathrm{N}$ in both cases. Original: $a=2500/250=10.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Doubled mass: $a=2500/500=5.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, exactly half, confirming the prediction.

exam_questions.statement: A ball of mass $0.20\,\mathrm{kg}$ is struck so that the resultant force on it during the hit is $4.0\,\mathrm{N}$. Calculate the acceleration of the ball during the hit.
mark_scheme: Selects the correct rearrangement, $a=F/m$.
Substitutes correctly: $4.0/0.20$.
States the correct value and unit, $20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
common_errors: Substituting 0.20 as the force and 4.0 as the mass, swapping the two quantities.

exam_questions.statement: An object accelerates at $2.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ under a resultant force of $750\,\mathrm{N}$. (a) Calculate the mass of the object. (b) State the direction of the object's acceleration if the resultant force instead acted directly against its current direction of travel.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $m=750/2.5=300\,\mathrm{kg}$. (b) The acceleration would point in the same direction as the resultant force, that is, directly against the object's current direction of travel, so the object would decelerate.
mark_scheme: Rearranges $F=ma$ to make mass the subject: $m=F/a$.
Substitutes correctly: $750/2.5$.
States the correct value and unit, $300\,\mathrm{kg}$.
States that the acceleration direction follows the resultant force, opposing the direction of travel in this case.
common_errors: Assuming the acceleration must still point in the direction of travel because the object 'is still moving forward'.

challenge_questions.statement: Extended: Explain how the principles covered in "Force changes velocity" apply to a real-world situation. Include relevant equations and units in your answer.
challenge_questions.answer: A complete answer links the physics concepts from force changes velocity to practical scenarios, using correct equations, SI units, and scientific reasoning.
challenge_questions.full_solution:
Step 1: State the relevant physics principles from Force changes velocity.
Step 2: Identify a real-world application.
Step 3: Apply the equations with correct units.
Step 4: Evaluate your answer for physical reasonableness.

mcq.stem: A $4.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ object has a $30\,\mathrm{N}$ force acting forward and a $10\,\mathrm{N}$ force acting backward. What is its acceleration?

options.text: $7.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ forward
options.why_wrong: substitutes the single 30 N force into F = ma instead of first finding the 20 N resultant.

options.text: $2.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ forward
options.why_wrong: substitutes the 10 N backward force alone into F = ma instead of the resultant.

options.text: $5.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ forward
$10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ forward
options.why_wrong: adds the two forces together (40 N) instead of subtracting the backward force from the forward force.

mcq.explanation: Resultant $=30-10=20\,\mathrm{N}$ forward; $a=20/4.0=5.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ forward.

mcq.stem: Which set of units is correct for use directly in F = ma without any conversion?

options.text: mass in N, acceleration in m/s², giving force in kg
options.why_wrong: puts mass in newtons, which is the unit of weight (a force), not of mass.

options.text: mass in g, acceleration in m/s², giving force in N
options.why_wrong: uses grams for mass without converting to kilograms first, which would give a force 1000 times too large.

options.text: mass in kg, acceleration in km/h², giving force in N
options.why_wrong: uses a non-SI unit for acceleration, which would not combine correctly with kilograms to give newtons.

options.text: mass in kg, acceleration in m/s², giving force in N

mcq.explanation: F = ma requires SI units throughout: kilograms for mass and m/s² for acceleration give force directly in newtons.

mcq.stem: A skateboarder moving forward experiences a resultant force that acts backward. What is the direction of the skateboarder's acceleration?

options.text: Backward, the same direction as the resultant force.
Forward, the same direction as the velocity.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes acceleration must follow velocity rather than the resultant force.

options.text: Zero, because the skateboarder is still moving.
options.why_wrong: confuses a nonzero resultant force with a zero resultant; a nonzero resultant always produces some acceleration.

options.text: Sideways, perpendicular to the motion.
options.why_wrong: introduces a direction with no stated force acting in it; the resultant described is backward, not sideways.

mcq.explanation: Acceleration always acts in the same direction as the resultant force producing it, here backward, so the skateboarder decelerates.

mcq.stem: A resultant force of $12\,\mathrm{N}$ gives an object an acceleration of $3.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. What is the mass of the object?

options.text: $36\,\mathrm{kg}$
options.why_wrong: multiplies force by acceleration instead of dividing force by acceleration.

options.text: $4.0\,\mathrm{kg}$
$0.25\,\mathrm{kg}$
options.why_wrong: divides acceleration by force instead of force by acceleration, inverting the correct ratio.

options.text: $9.0\,\mathrm{kg}$
options.why_wrong: subtracts the acceleration from the force instead of dividing one by the other.

flashcards.front: What equation links resultant force, mass and acceleration, and what are the SI units of each?
flashcards.back: $F=ma$, with $F$ in newtons (N), $m$ in kilograms (kg) and $a$ in metres per second squared ($\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$).

flashcards.front: Which force do you substitute for F in F = ma when several forces act on an object?
flashcards.back: Always the resultant of every force acting on the object, never a single named force on its own.

flashcards.front: Does an object's acceleration always point the same way as its current velocity?
flashcards.back: No. Acceleration points in the direction of the resultant force, which can oppose the object's current velocity, as happens when something brakes.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between mass and weight, and which one appears in F = ma?
flashcards.back: Mass (kg) measures the amount of matter in an object and stays constant; weight (N) is the force of gravity on that mass. F = ma uses mass, in kilograms.

flashcards.front: The same resultant force acts on a light object and on a much heavier object. Which one accelerates more, and why?
flashcards.back: The lighter object accelerates more, because for a fixed resultant force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass: $a=F/m$.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Only one of several forces is substituted into F = ma, even when more than one force is acting.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A worked example often names one force prominently (such as 'the engine force'), making it tempting to use that number directly without first finding the resultant.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner substitutes a single named force into F = ma while the question also states a second, opposing force.
misconceptions.correct_model: F in F = ma is always the resultant force: every force acting on the object must be combined into a single resultant before the equation is used.
misconceptions.remediation: Before writing F = ma, require a written line finding the resultant of all the stated forces first, and only then substitute that resultant for F.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Acceleration always points in the same direction as the object's current velocity.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Most everyday examples of acceleration are speeding up in the direction of travel, so the two directions are rarely distinguished.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner assigns the acceleration the direction of the velocity rather than the direction of the resultant force, even when a braking force is described.
misconceptions.correct_model: Acceleration points in the direction of the resultant force. When that resultant force opposes the object's velocity, the acceleration points backward and the object slows down, even though it is still moving forward.
misconceptions.remediation: Work a braking example where the resultant is backward while the object still moves forward, and show the acceleration vector pointing backward.

misconceptions.why_it_appears: Mass and weight are often used loosely as synonyms in everyday speech ('how much does it weigh'), and both are closely linked by w = mg.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes 'kg' in a line where force is being calculated, or substitutes a weight value in newtons for mass in F = ma.
misconceptions.correct_model: Mass, in kilograms, measures the amount of matter in an object and does not change with location. Weight, in newtons, is the force of gravity on that mass and does change with the local gravitational field.
misconceptions.remediation: Before substituting into F = ma, require the units of every quantity to be written out and checked: mass in kg, force in N, acceleration in m/s².

common_mistakes.mistake: Substituting a single named force into F = ma when more than one force is acting.
common_mistakes.why: A question often draws attention to one force by naming it, which makes it tempting to use that number straight away.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always write a line finding the resultant of every stated force before substituting into F = ma.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving the acceleration the same direction as the object's current velocity rather than the resultant force.
common_mistakes.why: In most everyday examples the object is speeding up in the direction it is already moving, which hides the distinction.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State the direction of the resultant force first, then give the acceleration that same direction, whatever the object's current velocity is doing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using weight in newtons where mass in kilograms is required, or vice versa.
common_mistakes.why: Mass and weight are linked and often used loosely as synonyms in everyday language.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write the unit of every quantity next to its symbol before substituting: mass must be in kg for F = ma to give newtons directly.

exam_notes: Always show the resultant-force step explicitly before substituting into F = ma, even if the resultant looks obvious; this is where most marks are lost.
State the direction of an acceleration or force whenever the question involves more than one direction; a bare number is often only worth partial credit.
Keep mass in kilograms throughout; converting from grams or confusing mass with weight is a common and avoidable error.

summary.big_idea: For a fixed mass, the resultant force and the acceleration it produces are linked by F = ma and always point in the same direction.
key_points: F = ma uses the resultant of every force acting on the object, never a single force in isolation.
Mass in kilograms, acceleration in m/s² and force in newtons combine in F = ma with no conversion factor.
Acceleration points in the direction of the resultant force, which may oppose the object's current direction of travel.
The equation rearranges to a = F/m or m = F/a depending on which quantity is unknown.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Find the resultant force first, then apply F = ma; the acceleration it predicts always points the way the resultant points, not the way the object happens to already be moving.

03_Springs_extension_and_proportionality.title: Springs, extension and proportionality
03_Springs_extension_and_proportionality.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Describe a load-extension experiment for a spring and interpret its graph, including identifying the straight-line (proportional) region.
Calculate the spring constant k = F/x from data within the proportional region, and identify the limit of proportionality on a load-extension graph.

prerequisites.statement: Find the resultant of forces acting on an object, including recognising when a system is in equilibrium.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A hanging load stretches a spring only because the load's weight and the spring's restoring force reach a new balance; reading off that balance point depends on this idea.

prerequisites.statement: Find the gradient of a straight-line graph, including its unit, from two points on the line.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The spring constant is read directly from the gradient of the straight part of a load-extension graph.

prerequisites.statement: Convert a length measured in millimetres to metres.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Spring extensions are often measured in millimetres with a ruler but must be converted to metres before use in k = F/x, to match the newton and metre units of the spring constant.

diagnostic_items.question: A $200\,\mathrm{g}$ mass hangs at rest from the lower end of a spring. Taking $g=10\,\mathrm{N/kg}$, what is the size of the upward force the spring exerts on the mass, and how do you know?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $2.0\,\mathrm{N}$ upward. The mass hangs at rest, so the resultant force on it is zero and the spring's upward pull must balance the weight: $W=mg=0.200\,\mathrm{kg}\times10\,\mathrm{N/kg}=2.0\,\mathrm{N}$.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner uses the mass in grams as if it were already a force in newtons, instead of converting to kilograms and multiplying by $g$.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It cannot be found without knowing the spring constant.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner does not use 'at rest' as the evidence that the two forces on the mass are balanced.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: A load stretches a spring until the spring's upward pull balances the load's weight; reading a load-extension graph assumes the learner can see that balance.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Name the two forces on the hanging mass, state that 'at rest' means their resultant is zero, and only then calculate the weight from $W=mg$.

diagnostic_items.question: A straight line on a graph passes through the origin and through the point $(0.040\,\mathrm{m},\ 10\,\mathrm{N})$, with force on the vertical axis and extension on the horizontal axis. Find the gradient of the line and give its unit.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Gradient $=$ change in force $\div$ change in extension $=10\,\mathrm{N}/0.040\,\mathrm{m}=250\,\mathrm{N/m}$.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner divides the horizontal change by the vertical change, inverting the gradient.
The learner finds the right number but omits the unit, which is what gives the gradient its meaning as newtons per metre.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: The spring constant is read straight off the gradient of the straight part of a load-extension graph, so finding a gradient with its unit must already be secure.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Mark two points on the line, write the change in the vertical quantity above the change in the horizontal quantity, divide, and carry the units through the division.

diagnostic_items.question: A spring stretches by $35\,\mathrm{mm}$. Write this extension in metres.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner divides by 100, as if the reading were in centimetres.
The learner divides by 10 only, moving the decimal point one place instead of three.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Extensions are measured with a millimetre ruler but must be in metres before $k=F/x$ gives a spring constant in newtons per metre.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Recall that $1\,\mathrm{m}=1000\,\mathrm{mm}$, divide the millimetre reading by 1000, and check that the answer is a small number less than 1.

theory_blocks.title: How far does a spring stretch, not how long does it become
theory_blocks.body:
Hang a load on a spring and it gets longer. The useful quantity for describing this is not the new total length, which depends on how long the spring happened to be before you touched it, but the [[blue:**extension**]]: how much extra length the load has added.

Two equally stiff springs with different unloaded lengths end up with very different total lengths under the same load, yet show the same extension, because extension measures the stretch itself, separated from the spring's original size.

Measuring an unloaded spring's length first, and subtracting it from every later reading, is therefore not an optional extra step: it is what turns a length measurement into an extension measurement.

theory_blocks.title: F = kx and the spring constant
theory_blocks.body:
For loads within the straight-line region of a load-extension graph, the extension $x$ is proportional to the applied load $F$:

$$F=kx$$

where $k$, the **spring constant**, is the gradient of that straight-line region, in newtons per metre ($\mathrm{N/m}$). A larger $k$ means a stiffer spring: a given load produces a smaller extension.

Rearranged, $k=F/x$, which only gives a meaningful, consistent value of $k$ when both $F$ and $x$ are taken from a point within the straight-line region.

assets.caption: A load-extension graph: the straight proportional region runs from the origin to the marked limit of proportionality at (0.050 m, 10.0 N), whose gradient gives k = 200 N/m; beyond that point the line curves and the load is no longer proportional to the extension.
assets.purpose: Show both the straight region that gives k and the curved departure beyond the limit of proportionality on one true-to-scale graph.

theory_blocks.title: Measuring the experiment correctly
theory_blocks.body:
A reliable load-extension experiment follows this order: measure and record the spring's unloaded length; add a load and measure the new length;

calculate that reading's extension as new length minus unloaded length; repeat for a range of increasing loads; plot load (on the vertical axis) against extension (on the horizontal axis).

Converting every length to the same unit, usually metres, before calculating extension or plotting avoids a mismatch between a ruler reading in millimetres and a spring constant expected in newtons per metre.

For example, an unloaded spring of $120\,\mathrm{mm}$ that reaches $156\,\mathrm{mm}$ under a $9.0\,\mathrm{N}$ load has stretched by $156-120=36\,\mathrm{mm}=0.036\,\mathrm{m}$,

giving $k=9.0/0.036=250\,\mathrm{N/m}$ if that load lies within the straight region.

theory_blocks.title: The limit of proportionality is not the breaking point
theory_blocks.body:
The limit of proportionality is the load beyond which extension is no longer proportional to load: on the graph, it is the point where the straight line ends and a curve begins.

[[red:Past this point, equal increases in load no longer produce equal increases in extension]], so a single value of k calculated from a point beyond this limit does not describe the spring reliably.

This is a separate idea from the spring breaking. A spring loaded just beyond its limit of proportionality typically still returns close to its original length when the load is removed;

breaking happens, if at all, at a much larger load still. This additional distinction (the elastic limit, and permanent deformation beyond it) is not required at this level and is deliberately left out.

keywords.definition: The increase in length of a spring caused by an applied load: stretched length minus original (unloaded) length.
The force per unit extension of a spring, k = F/x, measured in newtons per metre (N/m); it equals the gradient of the straight-line region of a load-extension graph with load on the vertical axis.
The load beyond which extension is no longer proportional to load, marking the end of the straight-line region of the graph.
Describes two quantities whose ratio stays constant; here, load and extension within the straight-line region of the spring.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading off k.** Within the straight-line region of a load-extension graph, a load of $4.0\,\mathrm{N}$ produces an extension of $0.020\,\mathrm{m}$. Calculate the spring constant.
reasoning: Since the point lies in the straight-line region, $k=F/x$ gives a meaningful spring constant.
Substitute the values directly, since both are already in newtons and metres.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $200\,\mathrm{N/m}\times0.020\,\mathrm{m}=4.0\,\mathrm{N}$, which recovers the original load.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing extension by load instead of load by extension, which inverts the spring constant.

worked_examples.statement: **From lengths to a spring constant.** An unloaded spring has length $120\,\mathrm{mm}$. Under a $9.0\,\mathrm{N}$ load within the straight-line region, it stretches to $156\,\mathrm{mm}$. Calculate the spring constant in N/m.
reasoning: Find the extension: $156\,\mathrm{mm}-120\,\mathrm{mm}=36\,\mathrm{mm}$.
Convert the extension to metres before using it in k = F/x: $36\,\mathrm{mm}=0.036\,\mathrm{m}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $250\,\mathrm{N/m}\times0.036\,\mathrm{m}=9.0\,\mathrm{N}$, which recovers the original load.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Substituting the loaded length (156 mm) directly as the extension, instead of subtracting the unloaded length first.

worked_examples.statement: **Predicting an extension.** A spring has a spring constant of $150\,\mathrm{N/m}$ within its straight-line region. Calculate the extension produced by an $18\,\mathrm{N}$ load, and explain what must be true about this load for your answer to be valid.
reasoning: Rearrange $F=kx$ to make extension the subject: $x=F/k$.
This rearrangement is only valid if the 18 N load still lies within the straight-line (proportional) region; if it exceeds the limit of proportionality, k no longer describes the spring at that load.
worked_examples.solution: $x=18\,\mathrm{N}/150\,\mathrm{N/m}=0.12\,\mathrm{m}$, valid only if 18 N is within the spring's straight-line region.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $150\,\mathrm{N/m}\times0.12\,\mathrm{m}=18\,\mathrm{N}$, which recovers the original load.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using F = kx to predict an extension for a load that is explicitly stated, or shown on a graph, to be beyond the limit of proportionality.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading a graph.** A load-extension graph is a straight line from the origin up to $(0.050\,\mathrm{m},10.0\,\mathrm{N})$, then curves, reaching $(0.080\,\mathrm{m},14.0\,\mathrm{N})$. (a) Calculate the spring constant from the straight-line region. (b) Explain why $k=F/x$ calculated using the point $(0.080\,\mathrm{m},14.0\,\mathrm{N})$ gives a different, unreliable value.
reasoning: For (a), use a point within the straight region: $k=F/x$ there.
For (b), compare what $k=F/x$ would give at the curved point with the true spring constant from the straight region.
worked_examples.solution:
(a) $k=10.0\,\mathrm{N}/0.050\,\mathrm{m}=200\,\mathrm{N/m}$. (b) $14.0\,\mathrm{N}/0.080\,\mathrm{m}=175\,\mathrm{N/m}$, which is not 200 N/m,

because $(0.080\,\mathrm{m},14.0\,\mathrm{N})$ lies beyond the limit of proportionality, where extension is no longer proportional to load.
worked_examples.interpretation: If the spring were still proportional at $x=0.080\,\mathrm{m}$, the load would need to be $200\times0.080=16.0\,\mathrm{N}$; the actual load of only $14.0\,\mathrm{N}$ shows the spring is extending faster than proportionality predicts.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating 175 N/m as a second valid spring constant rather than evidence that the point lies beyond the limit of proportionality.

guided_exercises.statement: Within the straight-line region, a spring stretches by $0.015\,\mathrm{m}$ under a $3.0\,\mathrm{N}$ load. Calculate the spring constant.
hints: Make sure the extension, not a total length, is being used.
Use k = F/x.
Check by multiplying your k by 0.015 m to see if you recover 3.0 N.
common_errors: Dividing 0.015 by 3.0 instead of 3.0 by 0.015.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Make sure the extension, not a total length, is being used.

**Step 2 — Method:** Use k = F/x.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $k=3.0/0.015=200\,\mathrm{N/m}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check by multiplying your k by 0.015 m to see if you recover 3.0 N.

guided_exercises.statement: An unloaded spring measures $80\,\mathrm{mm}$. Under a $4.5\,\mathrm{N}$ load within the straight-line region, it measures $95\,\mathrm{mm}$. Calculate the spring constant in N/m.
hints: Subtract the unloaded length from the loaded length to find the extension in mm.
Convert that extension to metres before dividing.
Divide the load by the extension in metres.
common_errors: Using the extension in millimetres (15) directly in k = F/x without converting to metres, giving an answer 1000 times too small.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Subtract the unloaded length from the loaded length to find the extension in mm.

**Step 2 — Method:** Convert that extension to metres before dividing.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Extension $=95-80=15\,\mathrm{mm}=0.015\,\mathrm{m}$; $k=4.5/0.015=300\,\mathrm{N/m}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Divide the load by the extension in metres.

exercises.statement: Within the straight-line region, a load of $10\,\mathrm{N}$ produces an extension of $0.040\,\mathrm{m}$. Calculate the spring constant.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $250\times0.040=10\,\mathrm{N}$.

exercises.statement: A spring has a spring constant of $250\,\mathrm{N/m}$ within its straight-line region. Calculate the extension, in millimetres, produced by a $7.5\,\mathrm{N}$ load.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $250\times0.030=7.5\,\mathrm{N}$.

exercises.statement: A student calculates k using a data point that lies beyond the limit of proportionality on their graph, and gets a different value of k from the one found using points in the straight-line region. Explain why this happens and state which value should be trusted.
exercises.answer: The straight-region value should be trusted.
exercises.full_solution: Beyond the limit of proportionality, extension is no longer proportional to load, so F/x is no longer constant there and changes from point to point; only within the straight-line region does F/x give a single, reliable spring constant.

exercises.statement: Two springs are made from the same wire and material but have different spring constants: spring A has $k=120\,\mathrm{N/m}$ and spring B has $k=240\,\mathrm{N/m}$. Spring A stretches by $0.050\,\mathrm{m}$ under a certain load, both within their straight-line regions. Calculate that load, then calculate the extension spring B would show under the same load, and explain which spring is stiffer.
exercises.full_solution: Spring B stretches only half as far as spring A under the same load, so spring B, with the larger spring constant, is the stiffer spring.

exam_questions.statement: A student investigates a spring. The unloaded length is $200\,\mathrm{mm}$. Under a $9.0\,\mathrm{N}$ load, within the straight-line region, the length becomes $230\,\mathrm{mm}$. (a) Calculate the extension in metres. (b) Calculate the spring constant in N/m. (c) State one precaution the student should take when measuring the lengths to reduce error.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Extension $=230-200=30\,\mathrm{mm}=0.030\,\mathrm{m}$. (b) $k=9.0/0.030=300\,\mathrm{N/m}$. (c) View the ruler scale at eye level, directly in line with the pointer or end of the spring, to avoid a parallax error.
mark_scheme: Subtracts the unloaded length from the loaded length: $230-200=30\,\mathrm{mm}$.
Converts the extension to metres: $0.030\,\mathrm{m}$.
Calculates $k=F/x=9.0/0.030$.
States the correct value and unit, $300\,\mathrm{N/m}$.
States a valid precaution against parallax or scale-reading error.
common_errors: Forgetting to convert the extension from millimetres to metres before dividing, giving an answer 1000 times too small (0.30 instead of 300).

exam_questions.statement: A load-extension graph for a spring is a straight line from the origin up to $x=0.050\,\mathrm{m}$, $F=10.0\,\mathrm{N}$, after which it curves. At $x=0.080\,\mathrm{m}$ the load is read as $14.0\,\mathrm{N}$. (a) Calculate the spring constant from the straight-line region. (b) State, with a reason, whether the point at $x=0.080\,\mathrm{m}$ lies within the limit of proportionality.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $k=10.0/0.050=200\,\mathrm{N/m}$. (b) No: if proportionality still held, $x=0.080\,\mathrm{m}$ would require a load of $200\times0.080=16.0\,\mathrm{N}$, but only $14.0\,\mathrm{N}$ is measured, so the point lies beyond the limit of proportionality.
exam_questions.full_solution: The smaller-than-predicted load at this extension is exactly what identifies the curved region on the graph.
mark_scheme: Calculates $k=10.0/0.050=200\,\mathrm{N/m}$ from the straight region.
States that $x=0.080\,\mathrm{m}$ is beyond the limit of proportionality.
Calculates the load that proportionality would predict at $x=0.080\,\mathrm{m}$: $200\times0.080=16.0\,\mathrm{N}$ (or calculates $F/x=14.0/0.080=175\,\mathrm{N/m}$).
Compares: the measured 14.0 N is less than the predicted 16.0 N (or 175 N/m is not equal to 200 N/m), so the load is no longer proportional to the extension.
common_errors: Assuming the graph must be straight everywhere simply because F = kx was used earlier in the question.

exam_questions.statement:
A student hangs loads from a steel spring and measures the length of the spring each time. The unloaded length of the spring is $150\,\mathrm{mm}$. The results are shown below.

| load / N | length of spring / mm | extension / mm |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 150 | |
| 2.0 | 160 | |
| 4.0 | 170 | |
| 6.0 | 180 | |
| 8.0 | 190 | |
| 10.0 | 208 | |

(a) Copy the table and complete the extension column.

(b) Plot a graph of load (vertical axis) against extension (horizontal axis), and draw a straight line through the points that lie on one.

(c) State the load at the limit of proportionality, and explain how your graph shows it.

(d) Calculate the spring constant of the spring, in N/m, using the straight-line region of your graph.
exam_questions.answer:
(a) Extensions, found as length minus the $150\,\mathrm{mm}$ unloaded length: $0$, $10$, $20$, $30$, $40$ and $58\,\mathrm{mm}$.

(b) The first five points lie on a straight line through the origin; the point for $10.0\,\mathrm{N}$ lies above (to the right of) that line.

(c) $8.0\,\mathrm{N}$. It is the largest load whose point still lies on the straight line; the next point, at $10.0\,\mathrm{N}$, has a larger extension than the straight line predicts, so extension is no longer proportional to load beyond $8.0\,\mathrm{N}$.

(d) Using the point $(40\,\mathrm{mm},\ 8.0\,\mathrm{N})$ on the straight line: $x=40\,\mathrm{mm}=0.040\,\mathrm{m}$, so $k=F/x=8.0/0.040=200\,\mathrm{N/m}$.
exam_questions.full_solution: Check for (d): $200\,\mathrm{N/m}\times0.040\,\mathrm{m}=8.0\,\mathrm{N}$, which recovers the load. Check for (c): if the spring were still proportional at $10.0\,\mathrm{N}$ the extension would be $10.0/200=0.050\,\mathrm{m}=50\,\mathrm{mm}$, but $58\,\mathrm{mm}$ was measured.
mark_scheme: (a) All six extensions found as length minus the unloaded length: $0$, $10$, $20$, $30$, $40$, $58\,\mathrm{mm}$.
(b) Axes labelled with quantity and unit, load on the vertical axis and extension on the horizontal axis, with sensible scales.
(b) All six points plotted correctly.
(b) A straight line drawn through the origin and the first five points, with the $10.0\,\mathrm{N}$ point left off that line.
(c) States the limit of proportionality is at a load of $8.0\,\mathrm{N}$ (extension $40\,\mathrm{mm}$), because it is the last point on the straight line and the next point lies off it.
(d) Converts the extension to metres and calculates $k=F/x=8.0/0.040=200\,\mathrm{N/m}$, with the unit.
common_errors: Taking the limit of proportionality to be the largest load in the table ($10.0\,\mathrm{N}$) rather than the last load whose point still lies on the straight line.
Using an extension in millimetres in $k=F/x$, which gives $0.20$ instead of $200\,\mathrm{N/m}$.

exam_questions.statement: A student is given a steel spring, a clamp stand with a boss and clamp, a set of slotted masses of known weight, and a millimetre ruler. Describe how the student should carry out an experiment to collect the measurements needed to plot a load-extension graph for the spring.
exam_questions.answer: Clamp the spring so that it hangs vertically from the stand, and clamp the millimetre ruler vertically beside it, with a thin pointer fixed to the bottom of the spring so that it reads against the ruler scale. Record the pointer reading with no load on the spring: this is the unloaded (zero) reading. Hang the first slotted mass on the spring, wait until the spring is at rest, and record the new reading; repeat for a series of increasing loads in equal steps, recording the load and the reading each time. For each load, calculate the extension as the reading minus the unloaded reading. Read the ruler with the eye level with the pointer to avoid a parallax error, and take the readings again as the loads are removed one at a time to check that they repeat.
exam_questions.full_solution: The weights of the slotted masses give the loads in newtons; the pointer and fixed ruler turn an awkward measurement of a moving spring end into a single scale reading. The unloaded reading is what makes every later reading into an extension rather than a length.
mark_scheme: Spring hung vertically from the clamp stand with the millimetre ruler fixed vertically alongside it (a pointer attached to the spring to read against the scale).
Measures and records the reading (or spring length) with no load on the spring, before any load is added.
Adds known loads one at a time, in increasing steps, recording the load and the new reading each time.

Calculates the extension for each load as the new reading minus the unloaded reading, with one named precaution, for example reading the scale at eye level to avoid parallax or repeating the readings as the loads are removed.
common_errors: Describing only the loading, with no unloaded reading taken first, so lengths rather than extensions are recorded.
Giving a precaution such as 'repeat the experiment' without saying what is repeated or what it checks.

challenge_questions.statement: A spring's load-extension graph is a straight line through the origin for loads up to $12.0\,\mathrm{N}$, reaching an extension of $0.060\,\mathrm{m}$ at that load, and curves beyond it. A second, different spring has twice the spring constant of the first. If both springs are loaded with $9.0\,\mathrm{N}$, each still within its own straight-line region, compare their extensions without first calculating either spring constant explicitly in a separate step, then check your reasoning with a full calculation.
hints: Think about how extension depends on k for a fixed load, before calculating anything.
A spring constant twice as large should produce an extension some definite fraction as large, for the same load.
Calculate both spring constants and both extensions to confirm your prediction.
challenge_questions.answer: The second spring's extension should be exactly half the first spring's extension, for the same 9.0 N load, since extension is inversely proportional to k when F is fixed.
challenge_questions.full_solution: First spring: $k_1=12.0/0.060=200\,\mathrm{N/m}$; at $9.0\,\mathrm{N}$, $x_1=9.0/200=0.045\,\mathrm{m}$. Second spring: $k_2=2\times200=400\,\mathrm{N/m}$; at $9.0\,\mathrm{N}$, $x_2=9.0/400=0.0225\,\mathrm{m}$, which is exactly half of $0.045\,\mathrm{m}$, confirming the prediction.
common_errors: Assuming a spring with double the spring constant must stretch twice as far, rather than half as far, for the same load.

$230\,\mathrm{mm}$

options.text: Any point on the graph, since k = F/x always gives the same answer.
options.why_wrong: is false beyond the limit of proportionality, where F/x changes from point to point.

options.why_wrong: wrongly equates the limit of proportionality with breaking, which happens, if at all, at a much larger load.

The graph continues as the same straight line as before.
