mcq.stem: The same force is spread over a larger contact area. What happens to the pressure?

options.text: It increases.
options.why_wrong: reverses the correct relationship; for a fixed force, a larger area gives a smaller pressure, not a larger one.

options.text: It stays exactly the same, since the force has not changed.
options.why_wrong: ignores that pressure depends on area as well as force; changing the area changes the pressure even with the force fixed.

options.text: It decreases.
It cannot be predicted without knowing the material of the surface.
options.why_wrong: is unnecessary; p = F/A predicts the direction of the change from the force and area alone.

mcq.explanation: For a fixed force, pressure decreases as the contact area increases, since p = F/A and A is in the denominator.

mcq.stem: A block has a contact area of $0.020\,\mathrm{m^2}$ and a volume of $0.0060\,\mathrm{m^3}$. Which value should be used as A in p = F/A?

options.why_wrong: uses the volume, a three-dimensional quantity, in place of the two-dimensional contact area required by p = F/A.

options.text: The sum of the area and the volume.
options.why_wrong: combines two different physical quantities with different units, which cannot be meaningfully added.

options.text: Whichever of the two numbers is larger.
options.why_wrong: is not a valid rule; the formula specifically requires the contact area, not the larger of any two given numbers.

mcq.explanation: p = F/A requires the contact area in square metres; the volume, in cubic metres, is a different physical quantity and plays no part in this formula.

mcq.stem: A force of $40\,\mathrm{N}$ acts over an area of $0.0020\,\mathrm{m^2}$. What is the correct value and unit for the resulting pressure?

options.why_wrong: calculates the correct number but gives it the unit of force rather than the unit of pressure.
divides area by force instead of force by area, inverting the correct ratio.

options.text: $40\,\mathrm{Pa}$
options.why_wrong: ignores the area entirely and reports the force's numerical value with the unit of pressure attached.

mcq.explanation: $p=F/A=40/0.0020=20\,000\,\mathrm{Pa}$; the unit of pressure is the pascal (equivalently N/m²), not the newton.

mcq.stem: Two objects exert the same pressure on the ground. Object X has a larger weight than object Y. What must be true about their contact areas?

options.text: Object X must have a smaller contact area than object Y.
options.why_wrong: gets the relationship backward; a larger force needs a larger area, not a smaller one, to give the same pressure.

options.text: Object X must have a larger contact area than object Y.
Both objects must have exactly the same contact area.
options.why_wrong: would only give equal pressure if the forces were also equal, which they are not here.

options.text: The contact areas cannot be compared without more information.
options.why_wrong: overlooks that p = F/A directly predicts how the areas must compare, given equal pressures and unequal forces.

mcq.explanation: Since p = F/A is the same for both and X has the larger force, X must also have the larger area, so that the ratio F/A comes out equal for both objects.

flashcards.front: What equation defines pressure, and what is its unit?
flashcards.back: $p=F/A$, with force $F$ in newtons, area $A$ in square metres, giving pressure $p$ in pascals (Pa), where $1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{N/m^2}$.

flashcards.front: For a fixed force, how does pressure change as the contact area increases?
flashcards.back: Pressure decreases as the contact area increases, because the same force is spread over more surface.

flashcards.front: What is the key difference between area and volume in the context of pressure?
flashcards.back: Pressure uses the two-dimensional contact area, in square metres; volume is a three-dimensional quantity, in cubic metres, and never appears in p = F/A.

flashcards.front: Why can a narrow stiletto heel exert a far greater pressure on the ground than a much heavier elephant's foot?
flashcards.back: Pressure depends on force divided by area, not on force alone; the heel's contact area is so much smaller than the elephant's foot that the ratio F/A comes out larger for the heel despite the much smaller force.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Pressure increases when the contact area increases, for the same force.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A bigger area sounds like it should have a bigger effect of every kind, so it is tempting to link 'bigger area' with 'bigger pressure' by analogy with how a bigger force gives a bigger pressure.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts that spreading the same force over a larger area will increase the pressure, rather than decrease it.
misconceptions.correct_model: For a fixed force, pressure decreases as the contact area increases, because the same push is now shared over more surface. A snowshoe reduces pressure compared with a boot precisely by increasing the contact area for the same body weight.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare the same force spread over a small area and a large area side by side, calculating both pressures, to show the inverse relationship directly.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Volume is used instead of area when calculating pressure.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both volume and area are 'size' measurements of a three-dimensional object, which makes it easy to reach for whichever one is more familiar or more readily available.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner substitutes a volume, in units such as cm³ or m³, into the pressure formula in place of the contact area.
misconceptions.correct_model: Pressure uses the contact area, the two-dimensional surface over which the force acts, in square metres; a volume, in cubic metres, is a different physical quantity and has no place in p = F/A.
misconceptions.remediation: Before substituting, require the unit of the 'area' value to be checked explicitly: if it is m³ or cm³, it is a volume, not an area, and the question's data has been misread.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The unit of pressure is the newton.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Pressure is built directly from force, so it is easy to assume it keeps the same unit as the force used to calculate it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes 'N' as the final unit of a calculated pressure instead of 'Pa' or 'N/m²'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Force is measured in newtons; pressure, force divided by area, is measured in pascals (Pa), equivalently written as newtons per square metre (N/m²).
misconceptions.remediation: Require every pressure answer to carry its unit through the division explicitly: N divided by m² gives N/m², which is renamed the pascal.

common_mistakes.mistake: Predicting that a larger contact area gives a larger pressure, for the same force.
common_mistakes.why: It is tempting to assume that 'bigger area' always means 'bigger effect', by loose analogy with how a bigger force gives a bigger pressure.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that area is in the denominator of p = F/A: for a fixed force, a larger area always gives a smaller pressure.

common_mistakes.mistake: Substituting a volume in place of the contact area in p = F/A.
common_mistakes.why: Volume and area are both 'size' measurements of an object and are easy to confuse under time pressure.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check the unit of the quantity being substituted as A: it must be in square metres (or convertible to them), never cubic metres.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving a calculated pressure in newtons instead of pascals.
common_mistakes.why: Pressure is calculated directly from a force, so it is easy to assume the unit carries over unchanged.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write the unit through the whole calculation: newtons divided by square metres gives N/m², renamed the pascal.

exam_notes: Convert any area given in cm² to m² (divide by 10 000) before substituting into p = F/A; this conversion step is often credited separately from the final calculation.
State the unit of a calculated pressure as Pa or N/m², never N alone.
When comparing two pressures qualitatively, say explicitly which quantity (force or area) is being held fixed in the comparison.

summary.big_idea: The same force produces a different pressure depending on the area it acts over: pressure, p = F/A, increases as area decreases and increases as force increases.
key_points: Pressure is force divided by contact area: p = F/A.
The unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa), equal to one newton per square metre.
For a fixed force, a smaller contact area gives a larger pressure, and a larger area gives a smaller pressure.
Area, not volume, belongs in the pressure equation, and must be in square metres, converting from cm² (divide by 10 000) where necessary.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Pressure is force shared over area: the same force gives a bigger pressure over a smaller area, never the other way round, and the unit is the pascal, not the newton.

summary.big_idea: Use the key physics ideas and methods from forces and pressure accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: What is the force constant of a spring which is stretched (a) 2 mm by a force of 4 N, (b) 4 cm by a mass of 200 g? (Take $g = 10$ N/kg.)
exercises.full_solution: The force constant is $k = F/x$, with $F$ in newtons and $x$ in metres. (a) $x = 2\text{ mm} = 0.002$ m and $F = 4$ N, so $k = 4 / 0.002 = 2000$ N/m. (b) The stretching force here is the weight of the 200 g mass, found from $W = mg$: $m = 0.200$ kg and $g = 10$ N/kg, so $W = 0.200 \times 10 = 2.0$ N. The extension is $x = 4\text{ cm} = 0.04$ m, so $k = F/x = 2.0 / 0.04 = 50$ N/m.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Hooke's law, Q25

exercises.statement: The spring in the supplied diagram stretches from 10 cm to 22 cm when a force of 4 N is applied. If it obeys Hooke's law, what is its total length in cm when a force of 6 N is applied? A 28 B 42 C 50 D 56 E 100
exercises.full_solution: The extension produced by the 4 N force is $22 - 10 = 12$ cm $= 0.12$ m, so the force constant is $k = F/x = 4 / 0.12 = 33.33$ N/m (recurring). Since the spring obeys Hooke's law, extension is proportional to force, so for a 6 N force the extension is $x = F/k = 6 / 33.33 = 0.18$ m $= 18$ cm. The natural (unstretched) length of the spring is the original 10 cm reading, so the total length under 6 N is $10 + 18 = 28$ cm. This matches option A.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Hooke's law, Q26

exercises.statement: Jo, Daniel and Helen are pulling a metal ring. Jo pulls with a force of 100 N in one direction and Daniel with a force of 140 N in the opposite direction. If the ring does not move, what force does Helen exert if she pulls in the same direction as Jo?
exercises.answer: Helen exerts a force of 40 N (in the same direction as Jo).
exercises.full_solution: Because the ring does not move, it is in equilibrium, so the total force in one direction must equal the total force in the opposite direction. Daniel pulls with 140 N on one side. On the other side, Jo pulls with 100 N and Helen pulls with an unknown force $F_H$ in the same direction as Jo. For balance: $100 + F_H = 140$, so $F_H = 140 - 100 = 40$ N.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Hooke's law, Q27

exercises.statement: A boy drags a suitcase along the ground with a force of 100 N. If the frictional force opposing the motion of the suitcase is 50 N, what is the resultant forward force on the suitcase?
exercises.full_solution: The resultant force is found by subtracting the opposing frictional force from the applied force, since they act in the same straight line but opposite directions: resultant $= 100\text{ N} - 50\text{ N} = 50$ N, acting forward (in the direction the boy pulls).
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Hooke's law, Q28

exercises.statement: (a) What resultant force produces an acceleration of 5 m/s² in a car of mass 1000 kg? (b) What acceleration is produced in a mass of 2 kg by a resultant force of 30 N?
exercises.full_solution: Using Newton's second law, $F = ma$. (a) $F = 1000\text{ kg} \times 5\text{ m/s}^2 = 5000$ N. (b) Rearranging, $a = F/m = 30\text{ N} / 2\text{ kg} = 15$ m/s².
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Hooke's law, Q29

exercises.statement: A rocket has a mass of 500 kg. (a) What is its weight on Earth where $g = 10$ N/kg? (b) At lift-off the rocket engine exerts an upward force of 25 000 N. What is the resultant force on the rocket? What is its initial acceleration?
exercises.answer: (a) $W = 5000$ N. (b) Resultant force $= 20\,000$ N upward; initial acceleration $= 40$ m/s².
exercises.full_solution: (a) Weight is found from $W = mg = 500\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ N/kg} = 5000$ N. (b) Two forces act on the rocket at lift-off: the upward thrust of 25 000 N and the downward weight of 5000 N found in part (a). The resultant (unbalanced) force is the difference between these, since they act in opposite directions: $25\,000 - 5000 = 20\,000$ N, directed upward. By Newton's second law, the initial acceleration is $a = F/m = 20\,000 / 500 = 40$ m/s².
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Hooke's law, Q30

exercises.statement: Explain the following using $F = ma$. (a) A racing car has a powerful engine and is made of strong but lightweight material. (b) A car with a small engine can still accelerate rapidly.
exercises.answer: (a) A powerful engine gives a large driving force $F$, and lightweight construction keeps the mass $m$ small; since $a = F/m$, both effects combine to give a very large acceleration. (b) Even with a modest force $F$ from a small engine, if the car's mass $m$ is small enough, the ratio $a = F/m$ can still be large, so the car can still accelerate rapidly.
exercises.full_solution: From Newton's second law, rearranged as $a = F/m$, acceleration increases if the driving force $F$ increases, and increases if the mass $m$ decreases. (a) A racing car's powerful engine supplies a large resultant force $F$ once air resistance and friction are overcome, and building the car from strong but lightweight materials keeps $m$ small. Because $a=F/m$, a large $F$ together with a small $m$ gives a very large acceleration - this is exactly what a racing car needs. (b) A car does not need a huge engine to accelerate rapidly if it is light: because $a=F/m$, a small force $F$ divided by a small mass $m$ can still give a reasonably large acceleration, so a lightweight car with a small engine can still accelerate quickly, even though its top force is modest compared with a bigger vehicle.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Hooke's law, Q31

exercises.statement: The weight of the uniform bar in the supplied diagram is 10 N. The bar is marked from 0 to 100 (in cm) and it rests on a pivot at the 40 cm mark (not at its centre). A separate downward force of 3 N acts on the bar at the 10 cm mark. Does the bar balance, tip to the right, or tip to the left?
exercises.answer: The bar tips to the right (clockwise moment 1.0 N m > anticlockwise moment 0.9 N m).
exercises.full_solution: Take moments about the pivot at the 40 cm mark. Because the bar is uniform, its weight (10 N) acts at its centre, the 50 cm mark, which is $50-40=10$ cm $=0.10$ m to the right of the pivot. This gives a clockwise moment of $10\text{ N}\times0.10\text{ m}=1.0$ N m. The 3 N force acts at the 10 cm mark, which is $40-10=30$ cm $=0.30$ m to the left of the pivot, giving an anticlockwise moment of $3\text{ N}\times0.30\text{ m}=0.9$ N m. The clockwise moment (1.0 N m) is greater than the anticlockwise moment (0.9 N m), so there is a resultant clockwise moment of 0.1 N m: the bar does not balance and tips to the right. (A common mistake is to forget the bar's own weight: it acts at the centre of mass, which is not at the pivot here.)
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Moment of a force, Q32

exercises.statement: The metre rule in the supplied diagram is pivoted at its centre (the 50 cm mark). An unknown mass $M$ hangs from one end, 50 cm from the pivot, and a 100 g mass hangs on the other side of the pivot, 40 cm from it. If the rule balances, which of the following equations gives the mass of $M$? A $M+50=40+100$ B $M\times40=100\times50$ C $M/50=100/40$ D $M/50=40/100$ E $M\times50=100\times40$
exercises.full_solution: The rule is in equilibrium (balanced), so by the law of moments the clockwise moment about the pivot equals the anticlockwise moment about the pivot. Since weight is proportional to mass (both weights are multiplied by the same $g$), the masses can be used directly in place of weights in the moments equation, with the common factor of $g$ cancelling from both sides. The moment due to $M$ is $M \times 50$ (mass times its distance of 50 cm from the pivot) and the moment due to the 100 g mass is $100 \times 40$ (its distance is 40 cm). Setting these equal gives $M \times 50 = 100 \times 40$, which is option E. (As a check, this gives $M = 100\times40/50 = 80$ g, a sensible answer since $M$ is lighter than the 100 g mass but placed further from the pivot.)
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Moment of a force, Q33

exercises.statement: the supplied diagram shows three positions of the pedal on a bicycle which has a crank 0.20 m long, measured from the centre of the wheel (the hub) to the pedal. In position A the crank points straight up (the pedal is directly above the hub). In position B the crank points diagonally, roughly halfway between vertical and horizontal (the pedal is above and to the side of the hub). In position C the crank is horizontal (the pedal is level with the hub, directly to one side of it). If the cyclist exerts the same vertically downward push of 25 N on the pedal in each case, in which case, A, B or C, is the turning effect about the hub (i) $25 \times 0.2 = 5$ N m, (ii) 0, (iii) between 0 and 5 N m? Explain your answers.
exercises.answer: (i) 5 N m occurs in case C. (ii) 0 occurs in case A. (iii) between 0 and 5 N m occurs in case B.
exercises.full_solution: The turning effect (moment) of the 25 N force about the hub is $F$ multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the hub to the line along which the force acts (the vertical line through the pedal), not simply by the crank length itself. In case A the crank points straight up, so the pedal is directly above the hub; the vertical downward force at the pedal acts along a line that passes straight through the hub, giving a perpendicular distance of zero, so the moment is 0 - this is case (ii). In case C the crank is horizontal, so the pedal is level with the hub and offset from it by the full crank length (0.20 m); since the force is vertical, this horizontal offset is exactly the perpendicular distance, so the moment is the maximum possible value, $25 \times 0.2 = 5$ N m - this is case (i). In case B the crank is at an angle between vertical and horizontal, so the horizontal offset of the pedal from the hub is greater than zero but less than the full crank length; the moment is therefore somewhere between 0 and 5 N m - this is case (iii).
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Moment of a force, Q34

exercises.statement: Which of the following will damage a wood-block floor that can withstand a pressure of 2000 kPa (2000 kN/m²)? (1) A block weighing 2000 kN standing on an area of 2 m². (2) An elephant weighing 200 kN standing on an area of 0.2 m². (3) A girl of weight 0.5 kN wearing stiletto-heeled shoes standing on an area of 0.0002 m². Use the answer code: A 1, 2, 3 B 1, 2 C 2, 3 D 1 E 3
exercises.full_solution: Pressure is found from $P = F/A$ for each case, and compared with the floor's limit of 2000 kPa. (1) $P = 2000\text{ kN} / 2\text{ m}^2 = 1000$ kPa, which is below the 2000 kPa limit, so it does not damage the floor. (2) $P = 200\text{ kN} / 0.2\text{ m}^2 = 1000$ kPa, also below the limit, so it does not damage the floor. (3) $P = 0.5\text{ kN} / 0.0002\text{ m}^2 = 2500$ kPa, which exceeds the 2000 kPa limit, so this does damage the floor. Only item 3 exceeds the floor's pressure limit, so the answer is E.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Pressure, Q35

exercises.statement: (a) What is the pressure on a surface when a force of 50 N acts on an area of (i) 2.0 m², (ii) 100 m², (iii) 0.50 m²? (b) A pressure of 10 Pa acts on an area of 3.0 m². What is the force acting on the area?
exercises.full_solution: Pressure is calculated from $P = F/A$. (a)(i) $P = 50/2.0 = 25$ Pa. (ii) $P = 50/100 = 0.5$ Pa. (iii) $P = 50/0.50 = 100$ Pa. As expected, the same 50 N force gives a smaller pressure when spread over a larger area, and a larger pressure when concentrated on a smaller area. (b) Rearranging $P = F/A$ gives $F = P \times A = 10\text{ Pa} \times 3.0\text{ m}^2 = 30$ N.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Pressure, Q36

exercises.statement: A girl plans to take a walk across a muddy field. Which type of footwear should she wear if she does not wish to sink into the mud? A stiletto heels B wellington boots C ice skates
exercises.full_solution: Sinking into mud happens when the pressure the foot exerts on the ground ($P = F/A$) is high enough to push the sole below the surface. For a given body weight, pressure is reduced by increasing the contact area $A$. Stiletto heels concentrate the girl's weight onto a very small area, giving a very high pressure, so they would sink in easily. Ice skate blades are even narrower and are designed to cut into ice, not to spread weight over mud, so they would also sink in (and are not practical for walking anyway). Wellington boots have a wide, flat sole that spreads the weight over a much larger area, giving the lowest pressure of the three options, so they are the best choice to avoid sinking.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, 'Questions' box after Pressure, Q37
